edges.relationship: Lawrence invokes Charles Taylor’s interpretive social science to defend hermeneutic readings of personal testimony and socially constructed intersubjective meanings.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2022 reply, paragraph beginning “My defence there, and here” and note 35, explicitly anchors this defense in Taylor’s “Interpretation and the Sciences of Man,” cited in the Rabinow–Sullivan edited reader (1987), 33–81. Lawrence distinguishes reconstructing possible historical subjectivities from statistically representative samples, acknowledges lost interviews and insists on source criticism. This is a particular conceptual resource, not an endorsement of all Taylor’s work or an original Taylor reading. The 1987 manifestation is not asserted as the essay’s first publication; editor credit is separate. The exact printed page for this passage was not independently collated; the verified locator is the original publisher HTML paragraph and note.

edges.relationship: Feldman and Lawrence place Speaking for the People alongside Eley’s A Crooked Line as attempts to connect social structures and discourse.
edges.evidence_note: Joint 2011 introduction, 8 and note 25, explicitly identifies Lawrence’s 1998 book and says Eley’s 2005 book adopts a similar position on the interconnection of structure and discourse. David Feldman’s equal coauthorship is retained. This is the authors’ particular methodological comparison, not an asserted causal influence, identical arguments, personal collaboration between Eley and Lawrence or a new reading of either complete book. Their account also recognizes the gains of cultural history rather than rejecting it wholesale.

edges.relationship: James names Ibn Khaldun as a particular resource for teaching the philosophy of history as part of the humanities.
edges.evidence_note: Own November 1977 interview excerpt, published and edited by interviewer Alan Warhaftig in 2023, answer to “What are you teaching?”, says he devoted one or two sessions to Ibn Khaldun and praises his account of what history means. This records a discrete teaching resource, not demonstrated early formation, adoption of a whole historical system or a newly read original treatise. James identifies no title in this answer, so none is supplied. The separate October 1976 Minty Alley conversation is not assigned the 1977 date.

edges.relationship: Douglas identifies James’s intensive reading of Marx, alongside Trotsky and political encounters in Nelson, as part of his turn toward revolutionary historical writing.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Rachel Douglas, article 284, connects James’s reading of Marx and Trotsky in England with the research that produced the 1936 play and 1938 history, retaining Harry Spencer’s practical and political role. Her note 17 cites James’s Beyond a Boundary, 151; that original passage is not newly read here. This is explicit scholarly mediation, not a verified exact first-reading date or Marx as sole source. Existing historical-materialism group edge 264 remains distinct; no identity is collapsed between that tradition and the person Karl Marx.

edges.relationship: Douglas reads James’s active restoration of enslaved people’s historical agency through Trouillot’s account of how historical silences are produced.
edges.evidence_note: Douglas 282–283 and notes 11–13 explicitly builds on Trouillot’s active, transitive account of silencing to interpret James’s history and drama as a reverse process of unsilencing. This is Douglas’s retrospective methodological comparison, not James borrowing a 1995 book after his death, proof that Trouillot directly read James, identical theories or an assertion that all archival gaps can be filled. Fischer and Buck-Morss are separately credited in Douglas’s genealogy. Neither Trouillot’s original nor complete James books newly read.

edges.relationship: McKay challenges the extension of Valverde’s Toronto–Ottawa evidence into an undifferentiated English Canada while praising her methodological innovation.
edges.evidence_note: Own A Note on Region (2000), 92–93 and note 3, names The Age of Light, Soap and Water and questions its spatial scale, regional typicality and use of a part to stand for a whole. He calls the book pioneering and deserving of praise for its methodology, while suggesting that a Boston–Halifax axis might be more pertinent for some Atlantic questions. This is a specific geographical and historiographical objection, not rejection of moral regulation or a new reading of Valverde’s complete book. The article lightly edits an unpresented 1997 talk and is dated by its 2000 publication; Valverde’s earlier work is not treated as responding to McKay’s later framework.

edges.relationship: McKay argues that Cook’s deconstruction of regionalism leaves the category Canada insufficiently questioned.
edges.evidence_note: Own A Note on Region (2000), 93/note 4, explicitly identifies Cook’s Regionalism Unmasked (1983) and states this precise objection. The surrounding argument92–94 calls for scrutiny of national categories and scale as well as regional ones. This criticism coexists with Cook’s separate positive use of McKay’s wartime Atlantic history in edge_2692; it is not a blanket verdict on Cook’s career or a freshly audited reading of his 1983 article. The distinct later comment94–95/n7 on the joint Cook/R. Craig Brown national synthesis retains joint authorship and is not needed to infer the narrow new objection.

edges.relationship: McKay explicitly borrows Perry’s frame of Canada at the edges of empires when explaining its combined colonial and colonizing position.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 Breach interview, answer on Canada as colonizer and colony, names Adele Perry when borrowing this frame before developing his account of British and United States imperial constraints. This is a bounded conceptual resource in his retrospective explanation, not evidence that Perry originated every part of his liberal-order framework or caused the 2000 prospectus. He neither identifies an exact Perry title here nor claims a personal teaching relationship. Perry’s original books remain unread; McKay’s broad historical and political conclusions remain his own, rather than independent findings of this dossier.

edges.relationship: Harris uses Said’s account of European categories to explain how fur traders organized their opposition between civilization and savagery.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1997–98 article 59/n 39 calls Orientalism the original and most influential discussion of the categories described in the preceding paragraph. Harris applies this resource to traders’ conceptual coordination while distinguishing their circumstances from European legal sovereignty 58. This specific use coexists with his later criticism of giving cultural discourse excessive explanatory weight, already 1017; neither wholesale adherence nor a critique directed solely at Said is asserted. Original Orientalism and the complete 2004 article remain unread.

edges.relationship: MacDonald and Wynn with Barnes identify Innis’s spatial economy as a particular resource for Harris’s framing of the collective Historical Atlas of Canada.
edges.evidence_note: MacDonald’s complete 1990 review quotes Harris’s preface invoking Innis’s account of Canada’s long spatial development through staple trades and transport, and distinguishing its pattern from the United States. Wynn and Barnes 2023:3 independently describe the volume’s dedication to Innis for spatial economy and to Andrew H. Clark for settlement and the local region. The Atlas belongs to its many contributors and cartographers, including Geoffrey J. Matthews; Clark retains equal credit for a distinct pole. This is an explicitly mediated resource, not a new reading of the original Atlas preface or Innis, and not all contributors’ sole intellectual genealogy.

edges.relationship: Wynn and Barnes describe Harris’s engagement with Habermas, alongside Foucault and others, as sharpening his understanding while he brought social theory into historical geography.
edges.evidence_note: Wynn and Barnes 2023:3 place this engagement within post-Atlas discussions with UBC colleagues and graduate students, and cite Harris’s 1991 call for conversation between historical geography and social theory. Their explicit account of theoretical clarification supports a bounded, named scholarly resource. Foucault retains separate equal credit and his already 1018 specific use; no singular origin, direct teaching, personal contact or detailed adoption of every Habermasian concept is inferred. Harris’s complete 1991 and 2008 articles and Habermas’s originals were not available as actual bodies through the checked routes and remain unread.
